findings.title: Description issues instructions to the model
findings.detail: Description of "request_application" contains imperative instructions directed at the AI assistant rather than describing the tool. This is the core tool-poisoning technique.

findings.remediation: Treat the server as untrusted; the model may obey embedded instructions.

findings.title: Description uses pressure/override language
findings.detail: Description of "employer_growth" stacks urgency/override words (always, never). Legitimate tool descriptions rarely pressure the model to act or ignore prior guidance.

findings.title: Generic tool name can shadow trusted tools
findings.detail: Tool "search" uses a generic high-value name. When multiple servers load together, this can intercept calls meant for a trusted server.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta: untrusted input + private data + external sink
findings.detail: Server "agent-mcp" exposes tools that together enable an exfiltration flow. Untrusted content: get_job, check_jobs_open, fit_resume, employer_hiring_record, employer_growth, search, fetch · Private data: fit_resume, employer_hiring_record, key_status · Public sink: search_jobs, check_apply_support, request_application, fit_resume · Destructive: board_stats, debug_search.

evidence.snippet: Untrusted content: get_job, check_jobs_open, fit_resume, employer_hiring_record, employer_growth, search, fetch · Private data: fit_resume, employer_hiring_record, key_status · Public sink: search_jobs, check_apply_support, request_application, fit_resume · Destructive: board_stats, debug_search

findings.remediation: Do not co-install these capabilities under one trust boundary; an injected comment/email can steer the model to exfiltrate via the sink tool.
